newsitem.title: FRANCE: YACHTING-FRENCHMAN FINALLY WINS DISASTER-PRONE YACHTING RACE.
newsitem.headline: YACHTING-FRENCHMAN FINALLY WINS DISASTER-PRONE YACHTING RACE.

text.p: The solo, round-the-world yacht race in which Briton Tony Bullimore was dramatically rescued and Canada's Gerry Roufs disappeared was finally won on Monday by a Frenchman.

Christophe Auguin, aboard his vessel Geodis, crossed the line at the French resort of Les-Sables-d'Olonne at 0933 local (0833 GMT). He had taken 105 days, breaking the 109-day race record set in 1989 by another French sailor, Titouan Lamazou.
The other competitors are hundreds of miles behind.
The accident-prone third Vendee Globe Challenge, through lonely, towering seas fraught with dangerous icebergs, has confirmed its reputation as one of the world's most dangerous sports events.

Only seven of the 16 competitors are still in the race which skirts southern Africa, rounds Antarctica clockwise towards Cape Horn to end in Les Sables d'Olonne, on France's Atlantic coast, where it started on November 3.
Canada's Roufs has been missing for over a month. He was last in contact with organisers when in a remote Antarctic area between New Zealand and Cape Horn in some of the world's heaviest seas.
Bullimore and Frenchman Thierry Dubois were plucked from the sea by the Australian navy in dramatic rescues after their boats capsized southwest of Australia.
Another Frenchman, Raphael Dinelli, was rescued by fellow competitor Pete Goss and taken to Tasmania.
Most other competitors had to make for land after breaking equipment in collisions with unidentified objects or marine animals. Some of them, although disqualified, have resumed the race.
The accidents, and the costly and risky rescues, have triggered charges that the French-organised race was too dangerous and that yacht builders had sacrificed safety to speed.
